newsitem.title: UK: Why pay $1.50 for a 40c Russia share say traders.
newsitem.headline: Why pay $1.50 for a 40c Russia share say traders.

text.p: The world's largest natural gas producer, Russia's RAO Gazprom, is asking foreign investors to stump up more than four times what locals pay for its shares and some believe that is too high a price.
Morgan Stanley and Kleinwort Benson, leads for Gazprom's American Depositary Share (ADS) offering, said on Monday the deal would be priced at the equivalent of $1.40-$1.50 per share.
"It is quite simple mathematics, why pay $1.50 for something you can buy for less than 40 cents," said a Russia trader at a bank in London.

Gazprom shares were trading on the Russian Trading System at 39 cents by 1000 GMT on Tuesday, but the lead managers and the company said there was no relationship between the true value of Gazprom and its underlying shares.

They said that at no stage would the ADS, which are dollar denominated euroclearable securities with guaranteed settlement, become directly exchangeable with the underlying stock and that they represent a totally different security which reflects the true value of the company.

The leads and the company have also made much of the fact that Gazprom tightly controls trading in its shares in Moscow and just 1.22 million shares traded on Monday out of a total issue of 23.6 billion.
"It really is not that difficult to buy the stock. You can source it in Moscow. It strikes me that Gazprom and the leads are trying to gouge investors," said the share trader.
The deal, which will see one to one and a half percent sold by the end of October this year, is a prelude to the completion of the disposal of a nine percent stake overseas.
The sale of the remainder will start once the company has completed its accounts to international standards at this time next year and meets listing requirements for a U.S. exchange.

But bankers in London say that in any case, the establishment of a Russian depositary and the movement of stock exchanges towards international standards means that the underlying stock price will move towards that of the ADS.
They also note that at $1.40-$1.60 there is rather more downside for the international offering than there is room for appreciation.

"You are buying political risk on a big scale with Gazprom. Yes, it is closely linked to the present administration, but that could be as much of a problem in the future as it is an advantage now," said a senior syndicate manager in London.

The company's vulnerability was indicated last week when the tax authorities froze its bank accounts as a result of $2.8 billion owed in back taxes, although Gazprom says that it is owed more by state entities than it owes.

"Natural resources is about the only sector of the economy the taxman can tap. You cannot tap growth in the wider legal economy because there isn't any," said an analyst who declined to be named because of the sensitivity of the Gazprom issue.
Despite the the high price, most observers believed the issue would succeed, partly because of the desperation of some fund managers.

"We have heard talk of a $85 million order from one organisation. The basic thing is that fund managers are sheep and will do whatever their peer group is doing," said a syndicate manager at a major European bank.

Also, funds are cash rich, having raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Russia they now have nowehere to go in a stockmarket which traded just $5 billion for the whole of 1995, so Gazprom is about the only thing they can buy.
